subject: Nvidia's China share fell to 34%, Huawei hit 28%
bodyMarkdown:
If you own an S&P 500 fund inside your RRSP, you own Nvidia, and overnight we got the clearest count yet of how much of China it has lost. Reuters reported late Monday, citing an IDC report it had seen, that Nvidia's share of China's data centre AI chip market fell to 34 per cent in the first half of 2026.

## What the IDC count shows

Nvidia shipped 678,000 units into China in the first half, down 44 per cent from a year earlier. Huawei took 28 per cent of the market on 572,000 **accelerators**, the chips that do the heavy arithmetic behind training and running AI models, up from more than 300,000 in the same period last year. Total shipments came to 2.008 million units. Inside that number, GPU shipments fell 26 per cent to 991,000 while non-GPU accelerators rose almost 80 per cent to 1.016 million, so they now outsell GPUs in China by volume. Behind the two leaders the field is crowded: Alibaba's T-Head at 7 per cent, Cambricon at 5 per cent, Baidu's Kunlunxin at 4 per cent, Hygon at 3 per cent. Nine of the 11 Chinese chipmakers IDC tracks grew their shipments. IDC did not break out which Nvidia products that 34 per cent covers.

## The market grew while Nvidia shrank

Here is the part I keep turning over. China's compute buildout kept going. The money went to domestic suppliers instead. IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19 per cent this year even as GPU shipments fall 9 per cent. Beijing pushed that along. Reuters reported last November that new data centre projects taking any state money must use domestically made AI chips, with projects less than 30 per cent built told to pull out foreign hardware or cancel orders. Nvidia's own annual filing for fiscal 2026 says the company was effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data centre compute market, which is a rare sentence for a firm that size to put in writing. Washington set out to slow Chinese AI. Going by these numbers it slowed one American company's sales and handed Huawei the customers.

## Volume is not capability

Shipping a lot of chips and shipping good chips are different problems. Tom's Hardware reported that Cambricon is aiming at roughly 500,000 AI chips this year, more than triple last year's output, while flagging low manufacturing yields and tight supply of **HBM**, the stacked high bandwidth memory that sits beside a processor and feeds it data fast enough to keep it busy. Starve a big chip of HBM and it idles. That is the ceiling I would watch, because it decides whether Huawei's 28 per cent becomes 40 next year or stalls near where it is now. Chinese labs are also wiring together more silicon to finish the same training run, and that bill arrives as electricity and floor space. You can buy your way around a slower chip. It just costs more every month you keep doing it.

## The takeaway

Watch IDC's second half numbers, and specifically whether non-GPU accelerators hold their new lead over GPUs in China. Watch HBM supply out of Korea, since memory looks likelier to cap Huawei and Cambricon than chip design is. If you hold the AI trade through an index fund, treat Chinese demand as already gone from Nvidia's base case rather than upside waiting to come back, because Nvidia's own filing treats it that way. And when Ottawa talks about sovereign compute, the question worth asking is what the alternatives cost per watt, not just per chip.
